Subsequently a sealed cover dak of the Government Women's College, Barisal addressed to the complainant was received in his office on 30.10.79 containing a revised result of Barisal Roll No. F-104 with Board Office Memo No. 914 dated 22.10.79 addressed to the Principal of the said Women's College, Barisal under the signature of the Controller of Examinations of the said Board dated 22.10.79. The revised result of the said Suchitra Rani Ghosh was shown as noted below against each subject. 

 The revised result in question of the above candidate was referred by the Principal. Government Women's College, Barisal to the complainant for, clarification and confirmation. The complainant checked up the revised mark-sheet in question and found that the form itself of the revised mark-sheet does not tally with the prescribed form to the Board's Office. The memo number as well as the revised marks were false and the signature of the complainant was also forged. He examined the relevant records of his office and found that no such memo as mentioned in the revised mark sheet in question was issued from his office and as such the whole process appeared to him to be false and fabricated. On verification it was apprehended that the beneficiary Suchitra Rani Ghosh might have forged the signature of the Controller of Examinations, Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Jessore and prepared the false revised mark-sheet for her wrongful gain. It was further suspected that an organized gang of cheat and forger was working behind it and thereby hampering the administration and reputation of the Board. Hence, the Ejahar was forged implicating the said Suchitra Rani Ghosh and asking the Police to find out the gang of culprits actually responsible for committing the above offence. P.W. 20 Abdus Sattar, S/I of Police attached to the C.I.D. Camp, Jessore took up the investigation of the case. During investigation, he seized some papers as per seizure list from the office of the Board as well as from the possession of some of the accused. He also obtained some specimen signatures and writings from the accused appellants together with the specimen signature of P.W. I. the Controller of Examinations. Jessore Board and sent them to a hand writing expert P.W.6 Abdul Mumin Miah of C.I.D. Dhaka for obtaining his opinion by way of comparison. He also seized a type machine in this connection and examined witnesses under Section 161 Cr.P.C. and then on completion of the investigation and after receiving that expert's opinion having found a prima-facie case submitted charge-sheet under Sections 419/420/467/ 468/471 of the Penal Code only as against these 3 accused as well as against another accused Shamsul Huda and no charge-sheet was submitted, as against the said Suchitra Rani Ghosh and another suspect accused Alamgir as their involvement was not prima-facie found. The learned Sessions Judge Jessore thereafter received the case records and framed charge as against the said accused Khitish Chandra Das and Ansar Ali under Section 465 as well as U/S 471 of the Penal Code and as against accused Atiar Rahman and Shamsul Huda under Sections 109/465 and 109/471 of the Penal Code to which all of them pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. 

 4. At the cut-set Mr. Wahab the learned Advocate has taken me through the F.I.R. the charges the evidence the confessional statements of the accused, and other relevant exhibits and then through the impugned judgment and order of the learned Sessions Judge. Thereafter he seriously assailed the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence as against the appellants on various grounds. He has firstly raised the question of want of jurisdiction of the learned Sessions Judge to try this case. His contention is that all these convicts-appellants were public-servants at the time of trial of the case and the alleged offences being under section 465 or Section 109/465 or 471 of the Penal Code, all fall within the Schedule of offences annexed to the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 and as such the said offences were exclusively triable by a Special Judge vide Section 5 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. 1958. But the present case for the said offences alleged to have been committed by the accused appellants have not been tried by a Special Judge but by a Sessions Judge under the ordinary law without any sanction from the govt. which is illegal and without jurisdiction. 

 5. Mr. Md. Abdus Salam Mamun, the learned A.A.G. in reply to the said contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants of the other hand submits that this question of jurisdiction of the trial court for the first time has been raised by the learned Advocate for the appellants in this appeal which is not proper. He however submits that the question of jurisdiction and for that matter, the question of sanction if any in this case ought to have been raised at the earliest stage before the trial court for proper adjudication. His further contention is that to examine the propriety and merit of the said submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants, it has to be first determined whether the accused appellants were at all public servants at the time of the commission of the alleged crime and trial of the same and secondly whether the alleged offences in fact fall within the schedule of offences as described in the Criminal Law amendment Act, 1958. Further submission of the learned A.A.G. is that admittedly the trial has been held by the learned Sessions Judge. Jessore who is in fact an ex-officio Sr. Special Judge being appointed vide the general Gazette notification No. 3498-J dated the 24th Oct. 1958 which was in the following term:- 

 In exercise of the powers conferred by Sub-section (2) of Section 4 of the Pakistan Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1985 (Act XL of 1958) the Government is pleased to direct that all Sessions Judges of East Pakistan be the Senior Special Judges in respect of their respective Sessions Division. 

 It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the State that the above notification has been adopted in Bangladesh and is still in force and applicable to the case of all the Sessions Judges of their respective Sessions' Divisions in Bangladesh. Now in this connection the learned A.A.G. also referred to Section 6 (B) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 as amended by Act XIII of 1987 to the following effect:- 

 6. Hence, according to the learned A.A.G, even if the alleged offences are found to be the Schedule offences under the Criminal Law Amendment. 1958 and are triable exclusively by the Special Judge, still then there has been no illegality in the trial of this case as the learned Sessions Judge is ex-officio Sr. Special Judge by operation of law and he took cognizance of the offences in this particular case on the basis of a Police report as required under the law and the trial by the learned Sessions Judge could be deemed to be a trial by a Special Judge under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 though he has not been specifically designated in the judgment as Special Judge or the case has not been numbered as a Special Case. He further contends that there has been no question of any prejudice caused to the accused for such non-mentioning of the case number and the designation of the trial Judge as such and hence the trial in any view of the matter cannot be deemed to have been vitiated or without jurisdiction. Now, let me consider the above submissions of the learned Advocate on this question of jurisdiction of the trial court in this case though admittedly it was not raised before the trial court in any way. 

 7. There is no denial of the fact that the offences as alleged unless fall within the Schedule of offences appended to the Criminal Law Amendment 1958 there cannot be any question of trial of the accused by any Special Judge as a Special Case under the said Act. In the present case, we may, however, look into the provision of part (b) of the Schedule of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 which is as follows:-(b) Offences punishable under Section 403 to 409, 417 to 420, 465 to 468, 471 and 477 of the Penal Code and the attempts abetments and conspiracies in relation thereto or connected therewith. when committed by any public servant as such or by any person acting jointly with or abetting or attempting to abet or acting in conspiracy with any public servant as such." 

 Apparently, it is found that the present offences under Section 465 and 471 of the Penal Code and for abatement of the said offences as in this case fall within the schedule of offences in question but if the above provision of Part (b) of the schedule is carefully examined, it will be found that the first requirement for the trial of an offence under the said schedule is that the accused must be a public servant as defined in Section 21 of the Penal Code as amended and it must be shown thereafter that such public servant committed the alleged offences as described above as such that means in the capacity of a public servant. The word 'as such' bears special significance. It is clear that to bring the offences within the above Schedule it must be shown that the public servant has committed the above offence or offences while discharging his official duties or purported to have been discharging his official duties. The commission of the alleged offences as stated above must have a nexus with the discharge or purported discharge of his official duties. Then and then alone the offences as described above May be treated as the offences within the Schedule under the Criminal law Amendment 1958 permitting trial of the same by a Special Judge or Sr. Special Judge. If a public servant commits an offence, not in connection with the discharge or purported discharge of his official duties and functions, then such offence cannot be deemed to be an offence under the Schedule as described above and the public servant committing the offence or offences not as such cannot be tried under the special law but may be tried in an ordinary court under the general law in his private capacity and in such cases, the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 are not attracted and there is no question of trial by a Special Judge under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 or under Prevention of Corrupt Act. Act 11/47. In support of my above view I may refer to a decision In the case of Zainal Abedin Vs. The State, reported in 9 D.L.R. 640 wherein the words' as such has been interpreted as follows:- 

 And unless the conditions namely (1) the offence is committed by a public servant as such or (2) the offence as committed by any of the accused persons must have abetted the public servant as such are fulfilled, the offence under Section 465 or under Section 471 of the Penal Code or its abatement cannot be an offence under the Schedule of offences described in the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 and the same cannot be tried under the said Act as a special case. This view of mine also finds support from another decision in the case of Sayeed Hai Vs. State, reported in 20 D.L.R., (WP) 20. 

 8. Now, in the instant case from the allegations as made in the F.I.R. or in the charge, it does not appear that the accused appellants committed the offence of: forgery as alleged in the discharge or purported discharge of their official duties. Out of these 3 appellants, convict Ansar Ali is a security guard and convict Khitish Chandra is a sweeper in the office of Jessore Education Board and convict Atiar Rahman appears to be a time-keeper in the office of the Assistant Engineer Railway at Jessore. From mere designations of these convicts-appellants, it is cry difficult to say whether they were public servants at the relevant time according to law. For determination of the question of their such status some other factors require to be examined in connection with their service, particularly with regard to the terms and conditions of their appointments the mode of payment of their remuneration and the nature of work and functions etc. Further even if they were public servants, still it is to be seen whether they were public servants at the time of the commission of the alleged offences and at the time of their trial. These matters for determination are in fact meant for the trial Court. But now at this appellate stage, it is difficult to positively ascertain whether they were public servants at all or at the relevant time. Moreover, even if for the arguments' sake, they were public servants or deemed to be public servants, still then it has to be seen whether the allegations as brought against them prima facie show that they had committed the alleged offences under Section 465 or 471 of the Penal Code or for its abetment in the discharge or purported discharge of their official duties. It has been submitted by the learned A.A.G. that the accused appellants were not the public servants at the relevant time and they did not commit the alleged offences under Sections 465 and 471 and for abetment of the same in the discharge or purported discharge of their official duties. Hence, the conditions for bringing the offences under the Schedule as described in part (b) of the schedule of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958, have not been fulfilled. The offences charged as against the accused appellants, therefore cannot be treated as the schedule offences under part (b) of the schedule of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 and the question of trying these appellants for the said offences under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 does not arise at all in the facts and circumstances of the case. I have carefully gone through relevant provisions of law, the allegations made against the accused in this case and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the parties and I find much force in the submissions of the learned A.A.G, for the State but I find no substance in the sub-mission of the learned Advocate for the appellants. I therefore hold that the trial of the accused for the alleged offences by the learned Sessions Judge has been rightly held and the accused have not been prejudiced thereby and as such there has been no illegality in the same. 

 11. In the instant case P.W.1 Md. Mofizuddin, the Controller of Examinations of the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education. Jessore is the informant. The forged Result-sheet Ext. 6 & 7 was received in his office and he verified the same with the tabulation sheets and found that the revised mark-sheet was false and forged and his signature there on was also forged. He 'lodged the F.I.R. and proved the same as Ext. 1. P.W. 2 Abdul Wahed is the Assistant Professor of the Government Women's College, Barisal who was present in the teachers' room of the college when the false revised mark-sheet was received and opened in that office. He took part in the comparison of the said mark-sheet with the earlier one and found the difference. He thereafter carried a letter along with the revised mark-sheet to the Controller of Examinations of the said Jessore Education Board, for verification of the same. In his cross-examination he has stated that Suchitra Rani Ghosh was a student of the Government Women's College. Barisal. He also stated that Professor Nazrul Islam was in-charge of Principal of the College at that time. P.W. 3 Abdul Batik is a peon of the Government B.M. College, Barisal since 28 years. He identified accused appellant Ansar All in the dock. He has stated that when the Chairman or the Secretary went to Barisal, Peon Abdus Samad told him that if there was any plucked student, he might be brought to Jessore. Then he took Dilip, brother of the said plucked student Suchitra Rani Ghosh Bearing Roll No. F-104 to accused Ai lbd1 Ali at the Jessore Board office and after leaving him there he again left for Barisal. P.W. 4 S.I. Hafizur Rahman who received the complaint from the Controller of Examinations, Jessore Board on 8.7.80 and filled up the F.I.R. form and proved it as Ext. 2. P.W. 5 is S.I. Rajabuddin who was attached to the Kotwali P.S. Jessore on 9.7.80. The case was endorsed to him by the 0/C. Kotwali P.S. Jessore for investigation. He then visited the place of occurrence but thereafter the case was taken up by the C.I.D. for investigation. P.W. 6 is the vital witness in the case, one Abdul Momin Miah, a hand-writing expert of C.I.D. Bangladesh. He received the documents sent by the S.I. A. Sattar of the C.I.D. camp Jessore under Memo No. nil dated 13.10.80 in connection with Jessore Kotwali P.S. Case No. 14 (7) 80 for his opinion after examination and comparison of the hand-writings with the disputed writings and sig-natures. He received the revised mark-sheet in 2 sheets containing the typed copy of the writings in Bengali and the short signature marked by him as (1) Exts. A, A(1) , A(2), A(8). B. B(1), B(2) to B(5), C & C(1) respectively. (2) the disputed Bengali type specimen writings in 14 sheets marked by him as exhibits D to D(13). (3) Specimen forms of revised mark sheets in 3 sheets marked as E to E(2). (4) Specimen writings of Atiar Rahman in six sheets marked as exhibits F to F (5). (5) Specimen writings of Shamsul Huda in two sheets marked as exhibits G to G(1). (6) Specimen writings in the form of hand writing of Khitish Chandra in 3 sheets marked as exhibits H to H(2). (7) Specimen writings of Khitish Chandra Das in two sheets marked as exhibits K to KM. (8) Specimen type writings taken from the machine No. C 281015 in three sheets marked as exhibits L to L(2). (9) Specimen type writings on 4 sheets taken from the type writer No. F-13763 marked as exhibits M to M(3). (10) Specimen signature of Mr. Mafizuddin marked as exhibits N. (11) Specimen writing of Suchitra Rani Ghosh on two sheets marked as exhibits P to P(1). 12. After necessary examination and comparison with the writings of the documents, the H.W. Expert gave the following opinion. (1) the writings marked A series are not the product of the same type writer from which the writing marked L series have been taken. He further opined that the type writings marked 'A' series do not agree with the type writings marked in Specimen forms marked 'E to E(2)' in both general and individual characteristics of writings. The word মাধ্যমিক বোর্ড in the beginning of the 1st line মাধ্যমিক ও উচ্চমাধ্যমিক শিক্ষা বোর্ড, যশোর after 3rd line জেলা, ডাকঘর, প্রযত্নে etc. are found absent in the writings marked A series and there are print in writings marked E series, besides the writings marked F series are products by cycle-styled process in thick paper whereas the writings marked A series are from the type writer and on less thick paper.
